patterns.comment: A bare `{` is a compile error in Burxt: it must be `\{` or open an interpolation. Flag it here so the editor says so before the compiler does.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.unescaped-brace.burxt

patterns.comment: The escapes Burxt actually accepts. Anything else is refused by the lexer. `\r` and `\0` were added in v0.0.176 and were missing here — the keyword parity test cannot see an escape, so this drifted silently.
patterns.name: constant.character.escape.burxt

patterns.comment: `{expr}` inside a string literal: an ordinary Burxt expression.
patterns.name: meta.interpolation.burxt

patterns.comment: Money literal: $19.99. Exact, scaled, never a float.
patterns.name: constant.numeric.money.burxt

patterns.comment: Percent literal: 8.25% — two more decimal places than written.
patterns.name: constant.numeric.percent.burxt

patterns.comment: Decimal literal: exact scaled integer, never IEEE-754.
patterns.name: constant.numeric.decimal.burxt

patterns.comment: The eight spellings Burxt used to have. They are still RESERVED WORDS in the compiler, but only so it can name the replacement: `fn` -> `function`, `mut` -> `mutable`, `impl` -> `implement`, `dyn` -> `dynamic`, `extern` -> `external`, `struct` -> `class`, `trait` -> `interface`, `record` -> `class`. A program using one of them does not compile, so the editor must not colour it like a keyword — it is an error, and this says so before the compiler does. (`enum` was NOT renamed.) `trait` and `record` were missing here: they live in the lexer's `renamed_keyword`, not in its keyword TABLE, so the parity test never asked for them.
patterns.name: invalid.deprecated.burxt

patterns.comment: `main` is a name the language owns. Burxt has no entry point — the whole file is the program — so `function main()` looks like one and is not one, which the compiler calls out as a trap rather than a crash. It is refused, so it is coloured as refused.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.reserved-name.burxt

patterns.comment: Method declaration: function (self: Type) name(...), with the receiver's type arguments when the class is generic — function (mutable self: Stack<T>) push_one(...)
Method declaration with the receiver's type left to the `implement` header: function (self) name(...) or function (mutable self) name(...). Shipped v0.0.95.
Function declaration, including `external function`.
Nominal type declarations.
implement Trait for Type
A region is a named allocation scope: the name is a binding, not a type.
let / let mutable bindings.
Decimal<Scale> or Decimal<Scale, Rounding> — the rounding contract is part of the type.
Built-in scalar types. CInt, CDouble, CPointer and the fixed widths i32/u8/u32/u64 exist only at the C boundary.
patterns.name: support.type.primitive.burxt

patterns.comment: `dynamic Trait` is the only syntax that asks for runtime dispatch.
A boundary marshaller: `amount: Decimal<2> as scaled`.
Type position after a colon, and named types in general.
patterns.name: entity.name.type.burxt

patterns.comment: `return tail f(x)` asks for a GUARANTEED tail call: constant stack, or a compile error.
patterns.name: keyword.control.tail.burxt

patterns.comment: `-> T allocates` — this function builds values in its CALLER's region, so every call site needs one.
patterns.name: storage.modifier.allocates.burxt

patterns.comment: `pure function` — the result depends only on the arguments: no I/O, no FFI, no impure calls. Checked, not documented.
patterns.name: storage.modifier.pure.burxt

patterns.comment: `public function`, `public class` — reachable from a package that DEPENDS on this one. C2. The boundary is the package and not the file, because `use` concatenates sources into one buffer.
patterns.name: storage.modifier.public.burxt

patterns.comment: `requires` / `ensures` / `decreases` — contract clauses on a signature, checked at runtime and quoted back when they fail.
patterns.name: keyword.other.contract.burxt

patterns.comment: `touches files, network` — what a function is allowed to reach. Contextual, so the keyword parity test never asked for it, which is why it went unhighlighted.
patterns.name: keyword.other.effects.burxt

patterns.comment: The six effects a signature may name. Only these; the compiler refuses any other word.
patterns.name: support.constant.effect.burxt

patterns.comment: `result` — the returned value, in scope only inside an `ensures` clause.
patterns.name: variable.language.result.burxt

patterns.comment: `it` — the subject of a contract bracket, `Int [> 0, <= it * 2]`. Special only there, and an ordinary name everywhere else.
patterns.name: variable.language.it.burxt

patterns.comment: Built-in functions. `print` is a statement keyword; the rest are calls.
patterns.name: support.function.builtin.burxt

patterns.comment: Method call on a receiver.
Field access.
Enum variant construction or match pattern: Enum.Variant
Plain function call.
patterns.name: entity.name.function.call.burxt

patterns.comment: `..` is the range in `for i in 0..n`, and its only legal position. Listed before the numbers can be reached, because `0..3` and `0.5` begin with the same two bytes and the decimal pattern must not swallow the dots — it does not, since `\d+\.\d+` needs a digit after the point, which is the same lookahead the lexer uses.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.range.burxt

patterns.comment: `=>` separates a match arm from its body.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.arrow.burxt

patterns.comment: One equality, no coercion: `==` compares values of the SAME type.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.comparison.burxt
